sections.h2: How does a foreclosure work in Florida?
sections.html:
Florida foreclosures go through a court. The lender files suit, a judge enters a final judgment, and the circuit court clerk sells the home at a public sale. The owner can stop that sale at several points, and one of them is a sale of the house on the owner's own terms.

The process rests on Chapter 45 and Chapter 702 of the Florida Statutes. Chapter 45 covers the sale itself and the right to cure, and section 702.10 covers a faster path some lenders use through an order to show cause.

A homeowner served with a complaint should study every date on it and speak with a Florida attorney soon. Delay seldom helps.

sections.h2: What happens after the judge enters a final judgment?
sections.html:
The judgment tells the clerk to sell the property at public sale. Under section 45.031, the sale takes place not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after the judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a later date.

Notice goes out on a website under section 50.0311 for at least two consecutive weeks, or in a newspaper once a week for two consecutive weeks. The clerk may run the sale electronically.

  • The top bidder puts up 5 percent of the bid as a deposit.
  • The clerk files a certificate of sale.
  • If nobody objects within 10 days, the clerk files the certificate of title and the sale stands confirmed.

The law treats the winning bid as sufficient consideration, so a later argument about price faces a hard road.

sections.h2: Can I stop a Florida foreclosure sale?
sections.html:
Yes, up to a point. Section 45.0315 lets the mortgagor, or the holder of a subordinate interest, cure the debt and stop the sale at any time before the later of the clerk's filing of the certificate of sale or the time stated in the judgment.

The cure is paying the amount stated in the judgment. If no judgment exists yet, the owner tenders the performance due under the security agreement, including accelerated amounts, plus the lender's reasonable expenses of foreclosing, which include reasonable attorney's fees.

The statute then closes the door: after that moment, there is no right of redemption. A homeowner who is counting on a post sale redemption period will not find one in this section.

sections.h2: What is the order to show cause route?
sections.html:
Section 702.10 lets a lienholder ask for an order to show cause by filing a verified complaint. The hearing may be held no sooner than the later of 20 days after service of the order or 45 days after service of the complaint.

The resulting judgment operates against the property only, and a deficiency may still be allowed where the law permits it. The statute also says attorney fees up to 3 percent of principal need no reasonableness hearing.

One limit helps owners who live in the home. The payment or vacate order does not apply to owner occupied residences, and a granted homestead exemption on the latest tax roll is a rebuttable presumption that the home is owner occupied. See section 702.10 for the full text.

sections.h2: What numbers and dates matter most?
sections.html:
The table gathers the figures from the statutes cited here. Dates run from the judgment or the certificate of sale, so use the clerk's docket for the real calendar in your case.

Florida judicial foreclosure timing from sections 45.031, 45.0315 and 702.10
ItemWhat the statute says
Sale after final judgmentNot less than 20 and not more than 35 days, unless the plaintiff consents to longer
Published notice of saleTwo consecutive weeks
Winning bidder deposit5 percent of the final bid
Objections after certificate of saleWithin 10 days
Show cause hearingNo sooner than the later of 20 days after the order is served or 45 days after the complaint reaches the owner
Right to cureUntil the later of the certificate of sale or the time set in the judgment

sections.h2: What happens to money left over after the sale?
sections.html:
If the sale brings in more than the debt and costs, the extra is surplus funds. The final judgment has to carry a notice about them, and a homeowner is told to check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.

Claims for surplus must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed. Other lienholders may also claim a share, so the clerk's file is the place to look before assuming anything is owed.

sections.h2: What should I do when I get a foreclosure complaint?
sections.html:
Read the summons for the response deadline and act inside it. A missed response can let the lender move toward judgment without your side being heard.

  • Collect the mortgage, note, payment history and any letters from the servicer.
  • Ask the circuit court clerk how to find your case on the docket.
  • Ask for the payoff in writing, since the cure under section 45.0315 depends on the amount in the judgment or the tender due.
  • Speak with a Florida attorney or a housing counselor before agreeing to anything.

Keeping a line open to the lender's attorney preserves choices, including a sale before the clerk fixes a date.

sections.h2: How do taxes and recording costs enter a foreclosure?
sections.html:
The certificate of title that follows a sale is on the state's list of taxable documents. Section 201.02(9) figures that tax on the highest and best bid at the sale.

Property taxes are separate. A change of ownership, including a foreclosure, resets the property to just value on the following January 1 for assessment, per the Department of Revenue's Save Our Homes guide. Owners who lose the home also lose the homestead exemption benefit, which is tied to permanent residence.

sections.h2: What does a sale before the auction look like?
sections.html:
A sale in the open market or to a cash buyer settles the lender's payoff out of the money at the table, and the foreclosure case can then be dismissed. A deed in that sale carries the stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 in most counties, and the state treats every party to the deed as liable whichever side agrees to pay.

The timing target is the sale date the clerk has set. If a buyer can close ahead of it, the owner avoids a sale at auction and keeps control of the price. If it cannot, ask the lender's attorney whether the sale can be postponed. The plaintiff may consent to a date longer than 35 days.

Have the title agent confirm the payoff, junior liens and unpaid property tax before you sign a contract.

sections.h2: What are my options before the sale date?
sections.html:
An owner facing foreclosure has several paths, and each one has a different effect on timing and cost.

  • Cure the debt under section 45.0315 before the cutoff.
  • Sell the house before the sale, which pays the lender from the proceeds and avoids a sale at auction.
  • Hand the lender a deed in lieu, a transfer the state revenue agency counts as a taxable deed.
  • Contest the case in court with an attorney's help.

Cash buyers often move quicker than a retail listing, which matters while the post judgment window is running. Call the clerk's office for the sale date, and get the lender's attorney to put the payoff in writing first.

faqs.q: How long after judgment is a Florida foreclosure sale held?
faqs.a: The sale is set for not less than 20 days and not more than 35 days after the final judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer period.

faqs.q: Is there a redemption period after the sale in Florida?
faqs.a: No. Section 45.0315 gives a right to cure only until the later of the certificate of sale or the time in the judgment, and then states that there is no right of redemption.
The circuit court clerk. The clerk may conduct it electronically, publishes the notice, files the certificate of sale and later the certificate of title.

faqs.q: What is the deposit on a foreclosure bid?
faqs.a: The high bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent of the final bid, and objections are due within 10 days of the certificate.

faqs.q: Can I get surplus money after the sale?
faqs.a: Possibly. Surplus claims must be filed before the clerk reports the funds as unclaimed, and a homestead owner should check with the clerk within 10 days after the sale.
